title: Malaria elimination happens one community at a time. Lao PDR is getting close to eliminating malaria. Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Nigeria, and Tanzania are also showing how local data can help… | Chris Elias | 10 comments
headline: Malaria elimination happens one community at a time.
post_text:
Malaria elimination happens one community at a time. 

Lao PDR is getting close to eliminating malaria. Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Nigeria, and Tanzania are also showing how local data can help countries make faster progress. 

Malaria can be prevented and treated, yet it still takes hundreds of thousands of lives each year. Young children and families with limited access to healthcare are affected most. 

New insights from Exemplars in Global Health show how countries are using local information to decide what will work best in each area. This approach, called subnational tailoring, looks at factors such as weather, mosquito patterns, access to healthcare, and local living conditions. 

By matching the response to the needs of each community, countries can use their resources more effectively and save more lives. 

Read more about how this approach is helping countries reduce malaria: https://lnkd.in/gP4wYCMZ

top_visible_comments.comment: Subnational tailoring is the ultimate blueprint for modern disease elimination. Moving past uniform, top down blueprints to match interventions with highly localized epidemiological variables like mosquito patterns and shifting environmental data is exactly how we optimize resource allocation and build true health systems resilience. A phenomenal showcase of data driven country owned public health strategy in action!

Malaria elimination increasingly requires precision at the local level. Combining surveillance with information on access, climate, and vector patterns can help direct limited resources where they can have the greatest impact, Chris Elias

Malaria elimination is ultimately a community-level outcome, and this is why locally led implementation must remain at the centre of the global malaria agenda.

Global strategies and national policies provide the direction, but sustainable progress depends on the capacity of health systems and frontline actors to translate those strategies into accessible, quality-assured services for communities.

Strengthening community engagement, ensuring consistent availability of essential commodities, improving the quality and use of routine data, supporting frontline health workers, and strengthening referral and accountability mechanisms are critical to closing the gap between policy and practice.

Equally important is building local capacity and ownership so that interventions are not only implemented effectively, but are sustained beyond individual projects and funding cycles.

The principle is simple but powerful: malaria elimination is not achieved by programmes alone it is achieved when health systems, communities, governments, partners, and frontline actors work together toward measurable and lasting impact.

One community at a time.

Yes, but it is not enough to eliminate malaria because SNT lacks the cross-border architecture, political command, and commercial efficiency needed to permanently eliminate a mobile parasite. Examples: micro-economic gaps, bureaucratic frictions, funding exhaustion.

title: Protecting yourself from HIV used to require a daily pill, and you couldn’t miss a single dose or the protection would stop. Now, there is a simple injection that protects you for six months at a… | Bill Gates | 384 comments
headline: Protecting yourself from HIV used to require a daily pill, and you couldn’t miss a single dose or the protection would stop.
post_text: Protecting yourself from HIV used to require a daily pill, and you couldn’t miss a single dose or the protection would stop. Now, there is a simple injection that protects you for six months at a time. In places where the barriers to accessing these preventive tools stack up quickly, this breakthrough is massive.

top_visible_comments.comment:
One pattern I’ve seen is that the strongest innovations don’t just improve outcomes.

They reduce how much those outcomes depend on perfect human behavior.

Reliability often improves when the system carries more of the burden.
That sounds good.  But of course, the surest way to avoid HIV infection is for single people to practice abstinence.   Why is this so difficult for people? Intimicy doesn’t have to be sexual.

Scientific innovation has a real impact when it translates into effective access for everyone. Advances in HIV prevention should be supported by public policies, adequate funding, and legal frameworks that guarantee the right to health, equal access, and freedom from discrimination. Prevention is also a matter of human rights.

What makes this so significant isn’t only the science, it’s reducing a daily burden that quietly determines whether prevention works in real life.

A breakthrough becomes real public-health progress only when it fits people’s lives, reaches the communities most affected, and remains affordable.
A huge step forward, but the distribution challenge in underserved areas just pivots from daily adherence to ensuring access for injections. That can be just as complex.

The injection is another step in the right direction, well, provided there are no unexpected side effects, such as hidden contraception or infertility.

The bottomline is that when it comes to casual sex, external protection like condoms is most reliable when people use them consistently. In reality, however, the more often the same pair meets for casual encounters, the greater their tendency to become complacent and engage in unprotected encounters. Familiarity breeds a false sense of safety, and condoms are more likely to be forgotten, abandoned or deliberately dispensed with the more they meet.

Meanwhile, HIV and other STIs remain relentlessly opportunistic, often requiring only a single unprotected encounter to infect. That's why I think this medication or any other development that expands access to prevention or treatment while reducing the burden of strict adherence to any regimen - particularly cumbersome treatment schedules - is a welcome development.

Bill Gates  Transitioning from daily oral regimens to long-acting bi-annual injections is a profound medical innovation that directly solves critical adherence challenges and expands global healthcare equity. Overcoming access barriers in vulnerable regions is essential for scaling transformative health solutions and safeguarding long-term public welfare.

From my base in Madrid, I closely monitor how philanthropic innovation and global health frameworks are integrated into large-scale sovereign development strategies. Serving as a trusted strategic agent and proxy for Ministers, Royal Family Offices, and UHNWIs across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia, my practice focuses on aligning visionary global initiatives with high-level operational execution on the ground.

A monumental advancement in healthcare accessibility and a vital step toward ending preventable health crises globally.

This is a remarkable medical breakthrough, and an equally important execution challenge. Innovation creates the possibility of protection, but access, affordability, reliable distribution, frontline healthcare capacity, and community trust determine whether that possibility becomes a real outcome. The greatest value will come when the people facing the highest barriers can consistently receive the protection without those same barriers following the innovation.

What strikes me is the behavioral shift as much as the medical one - daily adherence puts the burden of decision-making on the patient every single day, and a six-month injection removes that friction entirely. It’s a reminder that access isn’t just about invention, it’s about how many decisions a person has to get right to stay protected. Do you see this model - reducing decision points rather than just treatment cost - becoming the template for other chronic prevention areas?

Shifting from compliance-heavy daily protocols to biannual interventions is the single most effective unlock for global health delivery. The hardest part of medical innovation isn't inventing the molecule; it's engineering the delivery mechanism to match human reality in resource-constrained environments. Monumental step forward for compliance-driven prevention.

headline: A tool like AI Consult has exciting potential to act as a second set of eyes by reviewing doctors’ notes in real time.
post_text: A tool like AI Consult has exciting potential to act as a second set of eyes by reviewing doctors’ notes in real time. But to get the most out of these innovations, we need to measure real-world outcomes and ensure they’re actually benefiting the communities they serve.

The real promise of AI isn’t replacing human expertise — it’s making human decisions better. The same principle applies across industries: technology creates real value only when we measure its impact in the real world and improve people’s lives. Innovation needs outcomes, not just capabilities

AI——I often think of Leo DiCaprio in the Aviator “The way to the future”. Not sure if Howard Hughes actually said those words, but he lived it.

A four month old boy arrived at a Penda Health clinic in Nairobi with a fever and a blocked nose. A routine presentation on a busy morning. A yellow flag appeared on the clinician's screen. The heart rate was high for the child's age. She reached for her stethoscope, heard a murmur, and referred him. A congenital heart defect was confirmed and treatment began. That flag appeared inside the Easy Clinic EMR. Penda Health has run its clinical operations on our platform in Kenya for almost a decade. AI Consult was built on top of it, reading what the clinician enters as the consultation happens: the notes, the vitals, the diagnosis, the prescription. Penda Health and OpenAI conceived and led the programme. Easy Clinic was the technical partner that engineered and built the platform it runs on. Bill Gates points to the question that decides whether any of this matters. Are real world outcomes being measured, and are the communities served actually benefiting. That measurement begins with the record. Structured clinical data, captured the same way at every visit across an entire network, is what makes a randomised trial in primary care possible in the first place. It is also what makes the next one possible. Nine years in Kenya, and this is the work we keep returning to: build the foundation, so the evidence can follow. Congratulations to the clinicians at Penda Health and to the teams at OpenAI and PATH. Bill Gates Penda Health PATH OpenAI Robert Korom Gates Foundation

But if it has never been externally validated, is poorly calibrated, or fails in a different patient population, should we trust it in clinical practice? As clinicians, other factors need consideration if an AI model has to be adopted for use in clinical practice.

It makes me wonder if consumer products can become the "proof of progress" for industrial decarbonization. When people can literally experience innovation instead of just reading emissions reports, adoption becomes a cultural conversation, not just a policy one. 

That's a powerful shift.

Thank you for sharing!

The interesting lesson is that storage becomes investable when it is designed around the operating constraints of the customer, rather than around a technology label. In batteries we see the same: residual value, availability and the ability to redeploy an asset often matter as much as round-trip efficiency. The next step is making those lifecycle economics transparent enough for industrial buyers to act on them.

Excelente iniciativa! A adoção de soluções como as baterias térmicas da Rondo Energy demonstra como a inovação pode transformar processos industriais tradicionais em práticas mais sustentáveis. É inspirador ver grandes empresas como a Heineken investirem em tecnologias que reduzem emissões e promovem eficiência energética. Esse tipo de avanço reforça que a transição para um futuro de baixo carbono depende de parcerias entre indústria e inovação tecnológica.
The real breakthrough is making renewable energy available exactly when industrial processes need it. Reliability is what turns clean technology into scalable infrastructure.
The tricky part is measuring the actual footprint of what's in the glass. Sourcing, transport, packaging all add up before it hits the table.

This is a smart application of thermal storage.

Industrial heat is one of the hardest parts of the energy transition because factories need reliable high temperatures on demand. Using renewable electricity to charge heat batteries and then deliver steam when needed is a practical way to cut emissions without disrupting production.

Seeing a major company like Heineken test this at scale is encouraging. The more these solutions prove reliable and cost-competitive, the faster other industries can follow.

People rarely grasp the significance of this development. Heat makes up of approx. 50% of the energy demand and most of it is used by industry. Companies like Rondo and Newton Energy Solutions can really make a change in this piece of the energy puzzle.

Raise a glass to anyone who takes "lower emission" as a mission. But make sure that you lower it with enough care not to break it. Replacement will cost you nothing but costs the earth something. Be aware that glass industry needs massive amount of heat.

The real breakthrough here is not simply storing renewable energy—it is turning intermittent electricity into reliable, on-demand industrial heat exactly when production requires it.

That addresses one of the hardest parts of industrial decarbonization: factories cannot pause their processes and wait for the sun to shine or the wind to blow.

If thermal batteries prove competitive at scale, they could do more than reduce emissions—they could fundamentally reshape industrial energy economics.

The key question now is: how quickly can successful pilots like this become standardized infrastructure across energy-intensive industries?

Bill, this is a great example of how innovation in industrial heat - often overlooked compared to electricity - can unlock meaningful emissions reductions at scale. Using thermal batteries to decouple energy generation from usage timing feels like a practical and scalable path for heavy industries. What do you think will be the key factor in accelerating adoption - cost competitiveness, policy incentives, or proven reliability at scale?

title: Malaria Researchers Engineer New Bed Net Treatment | Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) posted on the topic | LinkedIn
headline: Malaria kills 600,000 people a year, most of them children — but #HHMIInvestigator Flaminia Catteruccia (Harvard T.H.
post_text:
Malaria kills 600,000 people a year, most of them children — but #HHMIInvestigator Flaminia Catteruccia (Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health) is opening a new front in the fight against it. Catteruccia and her team engineered two compounds that disrupt malaria parasites before they reach humans, and developed a way to apply the compounds to full-scale bed nets. In early tests, the approach worked. Mosquitoes showed no parasite development. This fall, volunteers in Ethiopia will sleep under treated nets during peak malaria season — a real-world test of whether the approach holds up outside the lab. Read more: https://bit.ly/4wE0LBW

Image credit: Kent Dayton

more_relevant_posts.post_text: Malaria remains a major public health challenge in Papua New Guinea (PNG) and accounted for most malaria cases and deaths in the Western Pacific Region in 2023. Despite current national efforts centred on insecticide treated nets (ITNs), there is a pressing need to explore supplementary vector control tools, given the resurgence of malaria in PNG since 2015, partly driven by declining insecticidal efficacy of ITNs. The Newly Adapted Tools and Network Against Mosquito Borne Disease Transmission (NATNAT) project is assessing the feasibility and acceptability of complementary vector control approaches in PNG communities and the health system. These tools include residual spraying, spatial emanators, and larval source management. 🔗 https://lnkd.in/g259uTz9 Zebedee Kerry Rachael Farquhar Kilon Manuv Paul Daly Stephen Bell, PhD Maria Ome-Kaius Moses Laman Professor Leanne Robinson Burnet Institute PNG Institute of Medical Research #NATNAT #GlobalHealth #Malaria #MalariaElimination #MalariaResistance #VectorControl #Community

Malaria: A Preventable Disease That Still Threatens Millions Malaria is a life-threatening infectious disease caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Despite being preventable and treatable, malaria continues to affect millions of people worldwide, especially in tropical and subtropical regions. Early symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, and fatigue. If left untreated, it can lead to severe complications such as organ failure and even death. The most effective ways to prevent malaria include using insecticide-treated mosquito nets, eliminating mosquito breeding sites, applying mosquito repellents, and seeking early diagnosis and treatment. Raising awareness, promoting scientific knowledge, and improving access to healthcare are essential steps toward a malaria-free future. #Malaria #PublicHealth #LifeScience #Healthcare #DiseasePrevention #GlobalHealth #Science #Research

Climate change is reshaping where and when malaria is transmitted, creating new challenges for malaria control. IVCC’s 2024-25 Annual Report explores how rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns and more frequent extreme weather events are altering malaria risk. Combined with insecticide resistance and shifting mosquito behaviour, these changes are increasing the need for new vector control tools. The Malaria Atlas Project estimates that climate change could result in an additional 123 million malaria cases and 532,000 deaths across Africa between 2024 and 2050. Extreme weather is projected to drive 79% of these additional cases and 93% of these additional deaths. Working with partners across industry, academia and public health, IVCC supports the development of resilient, adaptable vector control tools designed to respond to the evolving threat of malaria. Swipe through to learn more, then explore more in our 2024-25 Annual Report: https://lnkd.in/ey_PMJVm #VectorControl #ClimateChange #GlobalHealth

What if we could slow down mosquito resistance—and change the fight against malaria? New research led by Sebastian Horstmann is doing exactly that. Published in Scientific Reports, the study reveals how Fludora® Fusion-a powerful combination of deltamethrin and clothianidin-is helping to delay resistance in mosquitoes and strengthen long-term malaria control. 💡 Why this matters: Mosquito resistance is one of the biggest threats to malaria programs worldwide. Without new approaches, today’s solutions risk becoming less effective over time. The breakthrough? Dual-action chemistry. Not just killing mosquitoes-but outsmarting resistance before it spreads. In this article, discover: ➜ Why resistance is accelerating ➜ What’s really happening at a biological level ➜ How dual-action insecticides are changing the game ➜ What this means for the future of malaria control 📖 If you work in vector control, public health, or pest management—this is a must-read. Read the full article now: https://lnkd.in/dCC3a8JS #MalariaControl #Innovation #PublicHealth #VectorControl #FludoraFusion #Envu #ScienceMatters #Africa

Malaria is the deadliest climate-sensitive infectious disease. A new study finds that climate change has slightly increased childhood malaria overall. Looking ahead, rising temperatures could increase the malaria risk in southern and East Africa while reducing it where it is most rampant today, as it becomes so hot that even mosquitoes struggle to survive. The opposite is true for cooler regions where malaria isn't a significant problem today. In these areas, climate change is slowly making the temperature more suitable for mosquitoes to spread malaria, creating new challenges for communities that are less experienced at tackling the disease. This #PreventionWeb highlight was published in University of Chicago . 👉 https://lnkd.in/eET6Pq6J

The success of a malaria campaign isn't measured only by the number of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) distributed, it's measured by how well those nets continue to protect communities over time. That's why Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) is so important. Conducted every 9 months for three rounds, PDM provides evidence on: ✅ ITN presence in households ✅ ITN usage by household members ✅ ITN condition and continued effectiveness Beyond measuring coverage, PDM generates valuable insights that help strengthen future distribution campaigns, improve programme implementation, and reinforce behaviour change messages that encourage consistent use of mosquito nets. Quality data enables better decisions, stronger programmes, and greater accountability ultimately contributing to more effective malaria prevention and healthier communities. Every monitoring exercise is an opportunity to learn, adapt, and improve. #Malaria #PublicHealth #Zambia #ITNs #PDM #MonitoringAndEvaluation #DataForDecisionMaking #GlobalHealth #HealthSystemsStrengthening

How do you achieve deep, localized impact on a global crisis? Artem Volchenko , CEO of the SAFMI Foundation, is shifting the needle in Sierra Leone with the "Golden Fish Project." By deploying Gambusia fish directly into water systems, SAFMI isn’t just controlling mosquitoes, they’re building a self-sustaining, community-led infrastructure that measurably reduces malaria incidence. This is what real-world impact looks like: low-cost, community-owned, and highly effective. We discuss the science, the scaling challenges, and how they are creating a blueprint for sustainable disease prevention in our latest episode. 🔗Watch the full discussion: https://lnkd.in/dTZb6EF7 #ImpactInvesting #PublicHealth #SDG #SocialEntrepreneurship #GlobalDevelopment #SwissImpact

As the region advances towards #malaria elimination, zoonotic malaria has emerged as a growing concern, particularly in Southeast Asia. While P. knowlesi remains the predominant zoonotic malaria threat, growing evidence suggests that other simian Plasmodium species, such as P. cynomolgi and P. inui, may warrant greater attention amid increasing land use changes that drive zoonotic malaria transmission. Existing challenges in surveillance and diagnostics raise important questions about the true burden of zoonotic malaria and the ability of health systems to detect emerging threats effectively. In our latest article, we explore the hidden threat of other simian malaria beyond P. #knowlesi , the factors driving transmission, and what must be done to safeguard the region's progress towards a malaria-free future. Read more: https://lnkd.in/gah958BX #malariaelimination #AsiaPacific #SoutheastAsia #OneHealth

Why Malaria Is Still a Major Challenge in Africa Malaria continues to be one of the biggest public health challenges in Africa, affecting millions of people every year, especially women and children. Despite major progress in prevention and treatment, many communities still face difficulties due to mosquito breeding conditions, limited healthcare access, lack of awareness, and environmental challenges. Africa carries the highest burden of malaria cases globally, making prevention efforts more important than ever. Simple preventive measures like using quality mosquito nets, improving awareness, early diagnosis, and timely treatment can help protect families and save lives. At Indique Exports, we believe that access to reliable mosquito protection solutions can play an important role in creating healthier communities. By providing quality mosquito nets from India to Africa, we aim to support malaria prevention efforts and contribute towards a safer future. Malaria is preventable. Every step towards better protection, awareness, and healthcare brings us closer to reducing its impact. Together, we can protect communities, prevent infections, and help build a healthier Africa. 🌐 www.indique.in #MalariaAwareness #AfricaHealth #MosquitoNet #PublicHealth

headline: Curious about what we're building?
post_text:
Curious about what we're building? Watch to see how we're reimagining the refinery model for the next era of industry.

The Brimstone Rock Refinery turns one globally abundant rock into multiple essential materials—creating a more efficient, cost-competitive way to produce the foundation of modern life.

Thank you to Breakthrough Energy and Bill Gates for helping share our story.

more_relevant_posts.post_text: Today’s mining industry is where oil was in the 1880’s. Most of what is mined is wasted. At Brimstone we turn everything we mine into revenue. No more waste. No more tailings. No more digging up CO2. 4% of the global economy is about to get a lot more profitable.

Cement is one of the most important materials on earth, and one of the hardest to make with lower emissions. Brimstone in our portfolio is taking a different approach. Founder and CEO Cody Finke, Ph.D. explains how the company uses abundant rocks like basalt and silicate rock to produce the same Portland cement the world already uses, along with smelter-grade alumina and other valuable materials. The opportunity is enormous. Builders like Brimstone are making the materials modern life depends on more accessible, lower cost, and cleaner to produce.

Cement is all around us. It’s under your feet, in the buildings around you, and behind a lot of the infrastructure that makes modern life work. Cement is already cheap, trusted, and everywhere. That makes it hard to scale better, cleaner ways of producing it. Any new approach must compete with that reality. That's why I get excited by Breakthrough Energy companies like Brimstone that are pushing this work forward. Cody Finke, Ph.D. and the team are producing the same Portland cement the world already uses from abundant rocks like basalt and silicate rock, while also producing smelter-grade alumina and other valuable materials. The affordability piece is critical. Better materials only scale if customers can buy them, build with them, and keep costs competitive. Brimstone is taking on one of the biggest industrial opportunities out there, making essential materials more accessible, lower cost, and cleaner to produce.

🏗️ NEW DATA | Global Cement & Concrete Tracker Cement production accounts for roughly 8% of global CO2 emissions — most of which comes directly from clinker production in kilns. To map these emissions pathways, GEM’s expanded dataset now covers 3,884 plants worldwide and introduces plant-level kiln tracking. The latest GCCT dataset reveals critical shifts across global regional capacity, kiln fleet aging, and decarbonization progress: 🌏 Shifting regional growth: China's capacity expansion has effectively halted while India leads global development. 📆 Kiln fleet aging & emissions lock-in: China’s young fleet (averaging 18 years) risks locking in emissions through 2050, while aging fleets in the U.S. and Europe face urgent retirement decisions. 📉 Decarbonization levers lagging: Key direct reduction measures like clinker substitution and alternative fuels still have significant room to grow. 📖 Read the full analysis and download the new dataset: https://lnkd.in/eyxAU4cu

The Cement Industry is facing a "Limestone Reckoning." Here’s why. For over a century, cement production has been tethered to one core chemical reality: calcining limestone. It’s effective, it’s cheap, and it’s the source of roughly 60% of the industry’s unavoidable process CO2 emissions. But the status quo is shifting. I’ve been tracking the rapid evolution of **calcium-silicate-based cement production**, and the landscape has moved from "theoretical lab research" to "first-of-a-kind commercial demonstration." Innovators like **@Brimstone** are at the forefront of this shift, proving that we can produce high-quality cement without the massive carbon footprint of traditional calcination. **What’s changing?** 1. **From Limestone to Silicates:** Using minerals that don't contain carbon to produce standard Portland Cement (ASTM C150). 2. **Waste-to-Resource:** Companies are now looking at mine tailings as feedstock—turning environmental liabilities into building materials. 3. **The "Drop-in" Reality:** The goal is no longer just "green cement," but "drop-in" cement that meets existing safety standards, meaning we don't have to rewrite the building codes to start building lower-carbon cities. The transition is no longer just about chemistry; it’s about infrastructure, logistics, and capital. The companies that crack the code on scaling these silicate-based processes are the ones that will define the next century of construction. #Cement #Decarbonization #ConstructionTech #Sustainability #NetZero #Innovation #Brimstone

DID YOU KNOW.... Newfoundland and Labrador relies entirely on imported #cement . Sourced from Quebec or imported from overseas, this significantly raises the baseline cost of raw cement for local concrete producers, making the price subject to external markets, rising fuel costs, increasing tariffs and shipping rate flucuations. Baie Minerals Inc/BAIE Technologies Inc. is working to solve this problem with a Made-in-Newfoundland (net-zero carbon) cement and Supplementary Cementitious Material (SCM) binder that is upcycled from mine waste at the ATLANTIC CARBON MINERAL HUB in Baie Verte, NL. This #CircularEconomy solution mitigates environmental liabilities from legacy mine waste, boosts the local economy, displaces high cost imports and shields local construction from global supply chain shocks by providing a lower-cost domestic supply. #ConcreteSolution #WasteManagement #CementIndustry #AdvancedMaterials

In 1929, the Caterpillar® Sixty was built to do the heavy lifting that helped power agriculture, logging and construction across North America. This beautifully restored machine, purchased from the Hamilton family, was returned to operational condition by Finning's Saskatoon Service team and refinished by the Regina Service team. Its grey paint isn't just eye-catching, it reflects Caterpillar's original colour before the company adopted its iconic yellow in 1931. Powered by a 4-cylinder gasoline engine, the Sixty was a hands-on machine that demanded skill, strength and patience to operate. More importantly, it laid the foundation for what would eventually become the legendary Cat D8. While technology has transformed the operator experience over the last century, many of the core design principles remain. From the engine-forward layout to the fundamentals of its undercarriage, the DNA of today's track-type tractors can be traced directly back to the Sixty. Built to pull heavy loads rather than push a blade, the Sixty represented Caterpillar's early focus on agriculture and haulage applications. Nearly 100 years later, it offers a unique look at the origins of modern track-type tractors and highlights how key design elements have been refined and carried forward through generations of Cat machines.
